cases.title: Team number glued to a name
cases.why: '3팀김하나' glues a team label to the name; the digit boundary is the only cue that the name starts after 팀.

cases.title: Hangul given name followed by a Latin surname
cases.why: A single name that mixes scripts: Hangul given name then Latin surname, as in bilingual email signatures. The whole string is one span.
cases.text: Hello 민수 Kim, the report is ready.

cases.title: Hangul name annotated with its hanja form
cases.why: Hanja annotation in parentheses after a Hangul name is common in formal text; both forms are persons.

cases.title: Same given name in Hangul and Latin in one sentence
cases.why: Two mentions of one person written in two scripts, joined by 과; each is a separate PERSON span.

cases.title: A Hangul name and a Latin name in one list
cases.why: A list that mixes scripts: each name is its own span with the script change as an extra boundary cue.
cases.text: 참석자: 김민수, Maria Lopez, Chen Wei

cases.title: Mixed-script name followed by a parenthetical
cases.why: A mixed-script name followed by a parenthetical remark; the focus mixes Hangul and Latin.

cases.title: Hangul surname after the Latin title Dr.
cases.why: A Latin title abbreviation before a Hangul surname inside a Korean sentence.

ambiguity.note: A Latin title before a single syllable marks the syllable as a surname rather than the noun 박.

cases.title: Hangul name inside an English quotation
cases.why: An English sentence quoting a speaker who names a Hangul person; quotes and script boundaries meet.
cases.text: She said, "Please ask 이서연 about it."

projections_excluded.reason: The projection wraps the text in another pair of quotation marks, which would nest with the quotes this case is about and change what it tests.

cases.title: Hangul name inside an English sentence after a title
cases.why: A Hangul name in an English sentence with the Latin title Mr. before it; the span stays Hangul-only and the title is excluded.
cases.text: Mr. 김민수 will attend the review.

cases.title: Hangul person between a Latin acronym company and a Hangul company
cases.why: Companies named by Latin acronyms (LG) occur in Korean text; the acronym must not be mistaken for a person-like mixed token.

ambiguity.note: Both highlighted spans are companies that surround a motion-from-to construction.

cases.title: Hangul name followed by hanja in parentheses
cases.why: Hanja annotation after the Hangul name; both are PERSON spans for one individual.

cases.title: Hangul name with a parenthesized romanization
cases.why: The same person appears in two scripts in one phrase. Taxonomy convention: one PERSON span per form, excluding the parentheses.

cases.title: Hangul name followed by its romanization in parentheses
cases.why: The same individual appears twice, once in Hangul and once in Latin inside parentheses; both are PERSON spans.

cases.title: Hanja full name inside parentheses after a Hangul gloss word
cases.why: A hanja name in parentheses after a role word, common in formal records.

cases.title: Hanja full name followed by the object marker 을
cases.why: A hanja full name followed by a Hangul object particle: the script change marks the span end.

cases.title: Hanja given name written alone
cases.why: A two-character hanja given name with a Hangul particle and no surname.

cases.title: Han-script (hanja) name with a Hangul particle
cases.why: A Korean name written in hanja followed by a Hangul particle; the particle changes script exactly at the span end.

cases.title: Hanja name followed by a hanja-style title
cases.why: A hanja full name followed by the Hangul title 교수; the title is excluded.

cases.title: Hanja surname with Hangul given name
cases.why: A hybrid name: hanja for the surname and Hangul for the given name, which occurs in informal notation.

cases.title: Hanja name followed by Hangul reading in parentheses
cases.why: Reverse order: hanja first, Hangul reading in parentheses.

cases.title: Two hanja names in a list
cases.why: Two hanja full names separated by a middle dot with a Hangul noun after them.
cases.text: 金民秀·朴智恩 공동 연구팀이 선정되었다.

cases.title: Hangul name next to a fictional Latin-script company
cases.why: A Korean sentence containing both a Hangul person and a Latin company name; the company must not become a PERSON just because the sentence is mixed-script.

ambiguity.note: 'Works at X' marks the Latin string as an employer; 'Acme Robotics' has a company-style head noun.

cases.title: Latin given name with a Korean subject marker
cases.why: A romanized single-token name with 가: Latin script gives no information about which Korean particle follows.

cases.title: Latin given name followed by a Hangul surname
cases.why: A Latin given name followed by a Hangul surname, a bilingual user-profile style.

cases.title: Latin team letter before a name
cases.why: 'A팀의 최지훈' mixes a Latin letter with Hangul before the name.

cases.title: Latin name followed by Hangul in parentheses
cases.why: Reverse order of the parenthetical pattern: Latin first, Hangul in parentheses.

cases.title: Latin name followed by the Korean honorific 님
cases.why: A Latin-script name with a Korean honorific suffix after a space; the honorific is excluded.

cases.title: Latin-script foreign name followed by a Hangul particle
cases.why: A non-Korean Latin-script name followed directly by the Korean subject particle 가; script changes at the span boundary and the particle must be excluded.

cases.title: Latin-script name carrying a Korean topic marker
cases.why: A romanized name takes a Hangul particle; the particle is outside the span even though it follows Latin letters.

cases.title: Latin surname followed by a Hangul given name
cases.why: The reverse order of the previous case: Latin surname then Hangul given name, followed by a Korean subject particle.

cases.title: Mixed-script names in a comma list
cases.why: Two mixed-script names in a list; each mixes scripts internally, and the comma is a delimiter.

cases.title: Single name that mixes Latin and Hangul
cases.why: A mixed form such as 'Kim 민수' (Latin surname then Hangul given name) appears in informal text; the span contains both scripts and is one name.
cases.text: Please welcome Kim 민수 to the team.

cases.title: Name directly followed by a Latin abbreviation in parentheses
cases.why: The Latin abbreviation in parentheses is a country code, not a romanization of the name.

cases.title: Rare name glued to a team number
cases.why: A digit boundary before a rare name. The surname is uncommon in Korean, so name frequency gives no cue and the boundary must come from the structure.

cases.title: Rare name followed by hanja
cases.why: Hangul plus hanja annotation for a rare surname. The surname is uncommon in Korean, so name frequency gives no cue and the boundary must come from the structure.

cases.title: Rare name in Latin and Hangul in one sentence
cases.why: Two mentions of one person with a rare surname written in two scripts. The surname is uncommon in Korean, so name frequency gives no cue and the boundary must come from the structure.
cases.text: 회의록에는 Ong Jihu와 옹지후가 모두 나온다.

cases.title: Romanized name with a parenthesized Hangul form in an English sentence
cases.why: English sentence in which a romanized name is glossed with its Hangul form; both forms are persons, the parentheses are not.

cases.title: Latin place name inside a Korean sentence next to a Hangul person
cases.why: A Latin-script city inside Korean text: the Hangul person and the Latin place must be distinguished by role, not script.

ambiguity.note: 'Was born in X' with the locative 에서 marks the Latin word as a place.

cases.title: Romanized Korean name followed by the topic particle 은
cases.why: A romanized Korean name followed directly by a Korean particle. The hyphen and the script change both sit near boundaries.

cases.title: Hangul name with its romanization in parentheses
cases.why: Article 4 gives the romanized form of a Hangul name; the parenthesized romanization is a second mention of the same person, so there are two PERSON spans.

cases.title: One person written in Hangul, romanized and hanja forms
cases.why: Three renderings of the same name in one parenthesized series; each form is its own PERSON span and the commas and parentheses are delimiters.
cases.text: 김민수(Minsu Kim, 金民秀)가 대표를 맡았다.

cases.title: ALL-CAPS Latin surname followed by a Hangul given name
cases.why: A passport-style capitalized surname followed by the Hangul given name; the focus span mixes scripts.

cases.title: Year marker glued to a name
cases.why: '2024년박서연' without a space: the digit and 년 precede the name.
